name: p3-0207-udp-duties
title: Choosing UDP means doing TCP's jobs yourself, and what the kernel does not tell you
spec: Left panel 'When UDP fits': 'small request and response: DNS, NTP, DHCP, SNMP, syslog', 'latency-critical real-time media such as RTP, where a late packet is useless', 'multicast and broadcast discovery', 'carrier for protocols that bring their own reliability and congestion control: QUIC, RoCE v2 (NIC implements reliability), WireGuard, VXLAN and Geneve, game networking, StatsD'. Middle panel 'What the application must supply' (orange): 'retries and timeouts', 'sequence numbers', 'rate limiting', 'congestion control', 'keep datagrams under the path MTU: a single lost fragment loses the whole datagram; DNS used 512 bytes historically, EDNS(0) negotiates larger, QUIC aims for 1200 bytes or more'. Right panel 'Silent things': 'a full socket receive buffer silently drops datagrams: netstat -su receive buffer errors, nstat UdpRcvbufErrors; fix with net.core.rmem_max and SO_RCVBUF; ss -u -a -m', 'a datagram to a closed port draws ICMP port unreachable; only a connected UDP socket reports it as ECONNREFUSED on its next call, otherwise the sender never finds out', 'firewalls and NATs track UDP flows by timeout, typically 30 to 180 seconds: long-idle sessions such as VPNs and QUIC need keepalives'. Footer 'iperf3 -c 10.0.0.5 -u -b 1G -l 1400 -t 10 reports loss and jitter at the receiver; 0 percent in the lab but over 1 percent in production usually points at a policer, a shallow buffer or an unexpected bottleneck link'. Bottom bar: 'Unbounded UDP senders can overwhelm a network, which is why some operators rate-limit UDP'.
alt: When UDP fits, the duties the application must supply such as retries and congestion control, and the silent behaviours of receive buffer drops, ICMP port unreachable and NAT timeouts.
cap: Choosing UDP means supplying retries, ordering and congestion control yourself, and the kernel drops overflowing datagrams without telling you.

name: p3-0207-icmp-never-block
title: ICMP messages a firewall must never block, and what breaks if you do
spec: A table with columns 'Message', 'Needed for', 'If blocked'. IPv4 rows: 'type 3 code 4, fragmentation needed and DF set' 'Path MTU Discovery' 'no way to learn a smaller MTU; large transfers hang' (orange); 'type 11, time exceeded' 'traceroute (code 0 TTL expired in transit); code 1 is a fragment reassembly timeout' 'path tracing fails'; 'type 3 in general (net, host, protocol, port unreachable)' 'error feedback' 'senders wait for timeouts'. IPv6 rows: 'types 1, 2, 3 and 4' 'type 2 Packet Too Big is mandatory because routers never fragment IPv6; type 1 destination unreachable; type 3 hop limit exceeded' 'PMTUD and error feedback break'; 'types 133 to 137' 'router solicitation and advertisement, neighbour solicitation and advertisement (replace ARP), redirect' 'no addresses, no neighbours'. Side column 'Safe to restrict': 'rate-limit ICMP', 'block echo from outside'. Right panel 'Rate limiting by hosts and routers': 'net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit and icmp_ratemask; routers deprioritise ICMP handled on the control plane, so a hop showing * * * or high latency at one hop with normal latency after it is usually this, not a real problem'. Header strip 'ICMP rides directly on IP as protocol 1; ICMPv6 uses next-header 58; each message has a type and a code, and errors quote the start of the offending packet'. Bottom bar: 'Before you block any ICMP type on a firewall, check which of the types above it would break'.
anchor: ## 2. ICMP: the network layer's error and diagnostic channel
alt: A table of IPv4 and IPv6 ICMP types a firewall must not block, what each is needed for, and the failure when blocked, plus what is safe to rate-limit.
cap: Blocking type 3 code 4, time exceeded or ICMPv6 types 1 to 4 and 133 to 137 breaks path MTU discovery, traceroute, addressing and neighbour discovery.

name: p3-0207-ping-line
title: Reading a ping reply line: size, sequence, TTL and time
spec: Top: the reply line in monospace '64 bytes from 10.0.0.5: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=0.31 ms' with brackets. 'size: the request size plus 8 bytes of ICMP header', 'icmp_seq: sequence number, a gap such as 2 then 4 means a request or reply went missing', 'ttl: how many hops away', 'time: round trip'. Middle left a worked TTL box: 'Linux starts at 64, Windows at 128, network gear at 255. TTL 62 on a Linux host means 64 minus 62 = 2 routers'. Middle right 'First line: PING 10.23.2.1 (10.23.2.1) 56(84) bytes of data: 56 bytes of data, 84 with headers'. Lower: 'mdev, the variation in round trip time, hints at queueing: packets waiting in line inside a device'. Another example block with sequence 1, 2, 4, 5 and times 1.76, 2.35, 1.69, 1.61 ms with the missing 3 marked in orange. Rule strip 'ping sends only one packet per second by default, so packets should not arrive out of order; a reply over 1000 ms means an extremely slow link'. Option reminder 'ping -s 1472 -M do: payload 1472 + 8 ICMP + 20 IP = 1500 with DF set; -I eth1 forces the source interface; -6 for IPv6, link-local needs -I eth0'. Bottom bar: 'Ping answers only one narrow question: whether ICMP echo gets through'.
alt: An annotated ping reply line showing size, sequence number, TTL and time, with the TTL 62 equals two routers example and a missing sequence number.
cap: The TTL in a ping reply shows roughly how many hops away the target is, and a gap in the sequence numbers means a request or reply went missing.

name: p3-0207-ping-fail-source
title: A failed ping: the message and its source tell you where to look
spec: A decision tree starting 'ping fails'. Branch 1 'Destination Host Unreachable, with your own address as the source' leads to 'your host gave up asking for the neighbour's MAC: ARP or NDP failed on the local link, not routing' (orange). Branch 2 'Destination Host Unreachable from a router's address' leads to 'that router had no route'. Branch 3 'Destination Net Unreachable or Packet filtered' leads to 'routing or a filter'. Branch 4 'Request timeout, or no output at all' leads to 'dropped silently somewhere'. Right panel 'Ping has limits': 'ICMP can be treated differently from real traffic: low priority, blocked, rate limited, or hashed on to a different ECMP path', 'success does not prove an application can connect; test the port with nc -zv host 443 or curl -v', 'failure does not prove the host is down', 'some internet hosts disable echo replies so a site can load while ping gets no answer'. Bottom panel 'Practical jobs on a cluster': 'fping -a -g 10.0.0.0/24 or fping -f hosts to sweep nodes', 'ping -c 3 <peer rail IP> -I <rail NIC> proves each rail works', 'ping -M do -s 8972 <peer> verifies 9000-byte jumbo paths end to end'. Bottom bar: 'The source of the message matters as much as the message'.
alt: A decision tree of ping failure messages from Host Unreachable with your own address, to Host Unreachable from a router, Net Unreachable and timeouts, with ping's limits and cluster uses.
cap: Host Unreachable from your own address points at ARP or NDP on the local link, while the same words from a router point at a missing route.

name: p3-0207-trace-read
title: Reading a traceroute or mtr: noise versus a real fault
spec: Two eight-hop traces drawn as rows of numbered boxes. Upper trace 'Hop 5 prints * * *, hops 6, 7 and 8 reply normally': hop 5 box grey with the label 'router declined to answer the probes, or rate-limits TTL-exceeded replies: nothing is wrong here'. Lower trace 'loss starts at hop 5 and every later hop shows the same loss' with hops 5 to 8 in orange 'persistent to the final hop: genuine, at or after hop 5'. Rule box: 'a * * * at one hop matters little if later hops respond', 'high latency at one hop with low latency after it: control-plane deprioritisation of ICMP', 'loss at an intermediate hop that does not carry on to the final hop is rate limiting', 'only latency or loss that persists all the way to the destination is real', 'in the mtr pattern, one hot hop followed by clean hops is noise, a step that persists is a real fault'. Right panel 'How a trace is built': 'probes with increasing TTL or hop limit; the router that decrements it to 0 returns ICMP time exceeded (type 11) and reveals itself; the destination answers with ICMP port unreachable for UDP probes, echo reply for ICMP probes, SYN-ACK or RST for TCP probes'. Command strip 'traceroute -n 8.8.8.8 (UDP to high ports, 3 per hop)', 'sudo traceroute -I -n (ICMP echo)', 'sudo traceroute -T -p 443 -n example.com (passes firewalls that allow 443)', 'tracepath -n (no root, reports pmtu per hop)', 'mtr -n -r -c 100 8.8.8.8'. Bottom bar: 'When a trace looks wrong, check the forward path with mtr from both ends before you blame a router'.
alt: Two eight hop traces, one with a silent hop five and normal later hops that is noise, and one where loss persists from hop five to the end that is a real fault, with the reading rules.
cap: A silent or lossy hop that clears at later hops is control-plane rate limiting, while loss that persists to the destination is real.

name: p3-0207-trace-traps
title: Five ways a trace can mislead you
spec: Five cards. Card 'Asymmetric paths': 'traceroute shows only the forward path; the return path can differ and the round trip includes it; run mtr from both ends'. Card 'ECMP and load balancers': 'different probes may take different equal-cost paths, so you see hops from several routers or inconsistent paths; flow-aware tools keep the 5-tuple constant: paris-traceroute, dublin-traceroute, or mtr with fixed ports'. Card 'MPLS and tunnels': 'hops can be hidden when the TTL is not propagated, or label stacks shown'. Card 'NAT and cloud networks': 'virtual routers do not decrement the TTL or respond, so a cloud VPC trace typically shows only the first and last hops'. Card 'Probes are small, 60 bytes each' (orange): 'problems that affect only large packets, such as MTU problems, will not show up; use tracepath or ping -M do -s'. Centre small drawing of a path with a forward line labelled 'forward path (shown)' and a different return line labelled 'return path (not shown)'. Bottom bar: 'Use the right tool for the question: a trace shows hops, not the packet sizes that fit'.
alt: Five cards on how traceroute can mislead: asymmetric paths, ECMP, MPLS and tunnels, NAT and cloud hiding hops, and small probes missing MTU problems.
cap: Traceroute shows only the forward path, can be confused by ECMP, tunnels and NAT, and its small probes never reveal MTU problems.

name: p3-0207-overlay-mtu
title: Overlay MTU on a 1500 and a 9000 underlay: how many bytes each tunnel takes
spec: A horizontal bar chart. One bar per encapsulation, each bar the underlay MTU with the added bytes cut off, labelled with the remaining MTU for a 1500 underlay and a 9000 underlay. 'VXLAN: 50 added (outer Ethernet 14, often not counted, + IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8): 1450 and 8950' (orange). 'Geneve no options: 50, variable with options: about 1450 and 8950'. 'GRE: 24 (IP 20 + GRE 4): 1476 and 8976'. 'IPIP: 20: 1480 and 8980'. 'WireGuard: 60 on IPv4, 80 on IPv6: 1420 or 1400, and 8940 or 8920'. 'IPsec ESP tunnel: about 50 to 73, NAT-T adds 8: about 1400 to 1430, about 8930'. 'MPLS: 4 per label: 1496 per label'. Right panel 'Where mismatches bite': 'Kubernetes CNIs such as Calico (VXLAN or IPIP), Flannel and Cilium set the pod MTU from the underlay MTU and the overlay; a mismatch is a top cause of services work for tiny requests only', 'GCP VPC defaults to MTU 1460, configurable up to 8896', 'AWS supports 9001 inside a VPC but only 1500 across the Internet and on many inter-region and VPN paths: validate jumbo designs path by path'. Verify strip 'ip -d link show shows the mtu and the encapsulation device; then ping -M do'. Lab check values 'largest ping -M do -s payloads: 1472 IPv4, 1452 IPv6, 8972 jumbo'. Bottom bar: 'Compute, don't guess: overlay MTU is the underlay MTU minus the added bytes'.
alt: A bar chart of VXLAN, Geneve, GRE, IPIP, WireGuard, IPsec and MPLS added bytes and the resulting overlay MTU on a 1500 and a 9000 underlay.
cap: Each tunnel subtracts its added bytes from the underlay MTU, leaving 1450 for VXLAN and 1480 for IPIP on a 1500 underlay.

name: p3-0207-blackhole-steps
title: Finding and fixing a PMTU black hole: the step-down test and the order of fixes
spec: Left: the symptom list as small icons 'ssh connects but hangs after SSH2_MSG_KEXINIT', 'curl https hangs after Connected', 'a website loads only partly', 'git clone stalls', 'a small ping works while ping -s 1472 -M do fails', plus 'TLS handshakes with big certificates (the ServerHello flight) and scp of big files hang'. Middle: the step-down test as a descending staircase of sizes 'ping -M do -s 1472', '1452', '1432', '1400' with the last passing step marked 'largest that passes: the doorway width' (orange). Detect commands 'tracepath -n host shows pmtu per hop', 'ip route get host shows a cached PMTU', 'tcpdump -ni any icmp[icmptype]==3 and icmp[icmpcode]==4 shows whether need-frag messages arrive', 'tcp_mtu_probing: 0 off, 1 on after a black hole is detected, 2 always'. Right: ordered fixes from cleanest to roughest. '1 make MTUs consistent end to end, overlay MTU = underlay minus overhead', '2 allow ICMP type 3 code 4 and ICMPv6 type 2 through every firewall', '3 clamp MSS at the tunnel or NAT gateway: iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu, or nftables tcp option maxseg size set rt mtu', '4 tcp_mtu_probing=1 on the client as a safety net (Packetization-Layer PMTUD, RFC 4821)', '5 lower the interface MTU, last resort'. Footer 'Where black holes appear: VPNs, GRE, IPsec and WireGuard tunnels, VXLAN and Geneve overlays, cloud interconnects such as the GCP default VPC MTU of 1460, PPPoE, any firewall that drops ICMP'. Bottom bar: 'A black hole costs nothing for small packets and everything for big ones'.
alt: Black hole symptoms, a step-down ping test from 1472 to find the largest passing size, and the five fixes in order from consistent MTUs to lowering the interface MTU.
cap: Step down the ping -M do size to find the largest packet that passes, then fix by consistent MTUs, allowed ICMP, MSS clamping or probing.

name: p3-0207-jumbo-rules
title: Jumbo frames for AI clusters: the saving and the rules
spec: Left: two stacked bars of header overhead 'MTU 1500: about 3.5 percent TCP/IP overhead' and 'MTU 9000: about 0.9 percent'. Caption 'the same data in fewer, bigger packets cuts per-packet CPU cost and header overhead; storage and bulk transfers gain throughput'. Middle: the MTU stack 'host 9000', 'switch ports at least host MTU plus headers: 9216', 'RoCE v2 NIC MTU 4096 (InfiniBand MTU values 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096) inside an Ethernet MTU of 9000 or so'. Right: rules as a checklist. 'configure the MTU end to end', 'keep it consistent across hosts, switch ports, VLAN interfaces, bond members and the overlay', 'never mix MTUs within an L2 domain' (orange), 'test every pair of nodes with ping -M do -s 8972 or nccl-tests'. Failure note 'jumbo set on hosts but not on every switch port, or forgetting the encapsulation overhead for overlays and VPNs, causes black holes'. Bottom bar: 'Before you call a fabric ready, test every node pair at the jumbo size'.
alt: TCP/IP header overhead of about 3.5 percent at MTU 1500 versus 0.9 percent at 9000, the MTU stack of host, switch and RoCE, and the rules for end to end jumbo frames.
cap: Jumbo frames cut header overhead from about 3.5 to 0.9 percent, but only if every host, switch port and overlay uses the same MTU.

name: p3-0207-tool-by-question
title: Pick the probe by the question when ping and traceroute are blocked
spec: A two column table, question on the left, tool on the right. 'Does a TCP port answer, bypassing ICMP blocks? (SYN probes with RTT and flags)': 'sudo hping3 -S -p 443 -c 5 host, or sudo nping --tcp -p 443 --flags syn host (use only on networks you own or are authorised to test)'. 'Is the port open, TCP or UDP?': 'nc -zv host 22 443; nc -zvu host 53'. 'Does the whole stack work: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP?': 'curl -v --connect-timeout 3 https://host/'. 'Is the neighbour reachable at layer 2?': 'arping -I eth0 10.0.0.5'. 'Which nodes in a range answer?': 'fping -c3 -g 10.0.0.0/24'. 'What ICMP is crossing the wire?': 'sudo tcpdump -ni any icmp or icmp6'. 'What do the ICMP counters say?': 'ip -s -s neigh; nstat -az | grep -i icmp (InDestUnreachs, OutTimeExcds, InEchoReps)'. 'Where does the path stop through a firewall that blocks ICMP?': 'traceroute -T -p 443 or mtr -T -P 443'. Left-side ladder in orange showing ordering from 'port reachability' at the bottom to 'full stack' at the top. Bottom bar: 'Pick the tool that matches the question you need answered, and keep probing to networks you control'.
alt: A table pairing diagnostic questions such as is the port open, does the whole stack work and is the neighbour reachable with hping3, nc, curl, arping, fping and tcpdump.
cap: Each probe answers a different question, from TCP port reachability up to the full DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP stack.
